To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the excitatory drive to the canine I augmenting pattern neurons is supplied by glutamate receptors and the time-varying component is supplied by non-NMDARs and the tonic component is supplied by NMDARs.
the ionotropic glutamate receptor sub-types, N-methyl-D- aspartate and non-NMDAs, differentially contribute to the respiratory drive to canine inspiratory augmenting pattern neurons.

ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists, applied directly to canine medullary respiratory neurons, produce dose-dependent reductions in their spontaneous activity and that the effects of the antagonists on neuronal discharge frequency are different for the non-NMDa and NMDA receptors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synaptic mechanisms of inspiratory rhythm generation.
the mechanisms underlying the generation of respiratory rhythmic activity.
the role of glutamaterglic neurotransmission in the control of respiratory pattern generation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the canine medullary I augmenting pattern neurons receive excitatory synaptic drive from both NMDA and non-NMDARs.
both types of glutamatergics are important for the respiratory rhythm generation in the medullary respiratory centers.
both NMDA and non-NMDARs mediate synaptic input to canine medullary I neurons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

NMDA receptors are important in providing a tonic excitatory input to canine I augmenting pattern bulbospinal respiratory neurons and non-NMDAs receptors are important in supplying a time-varying augmenting input.
ionotropic NMDA and non-NMDARs are differentially involved in supplying excitatory synaptic drive to canine I augmenting pattern neurons.
ionotropic glutamate receptor subunits are differentially distributed and have distinct functional roles in the canine ventral respiratory group.
The main takeaway from our work is that
glutamatergics are important in the control of breathing and that the different types of glutamatergins (NMDA and non-NMDAR) are differentially involved.
ionotropic glutamate receptor subunits play different roles in supplying excitatory synaptic drive to canine medullary I neurons of the ventrolateral respiratory group.
glutamate receptors play a critical role in mediating the respiratory rhythm.
